sick.e: From Middle English sik, sike, seek, seke, seok, from Old English sēoc (“sick, ill”), from Proto-West Germanic *seuk, from Proto-Germanic *seukaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sewg- (“to be troubled or grieved”). The "very good, excellent" sense is an ameliorative semantic shift from the original sense of "in poor health".
Variant of sic, itself an alteration of seek.

sickle.e: From Middle English sikel (also assibilated in sichel), from Old English sicol, siċel, from Proto-West Germanic *sikilu, itself borrowed from Latin sēcula (“sickle”) or sīcīlis (“sickle”). Remotely related with English scythe and saw.
sickle.g: An implement having a semicircular blade and short handle, used for cutting long grass and cereal crops.

sickly.e: From Middle English seekly, sekely, siklich, sekeliche, equivalent to sick + -ly. Possibly a modification of Old English sīcle (“sickly”) and/or derived from Old Norse sjúkligr (“sickly”).
sickly.g: Frequently ill or in poor health; weakly.
In a sick manner; in a way that reflects or causes sickness.

sickness.e: From Middle English sikness, from Old English sēocnes, sēocness, sēocnys, sēocnyss. By surface analysis, sick + -ness.
sickness.g: The quality or state of being sick or diseased; illness; an illness.

side.e: From Middle English side, from Old English sīde (“side, flank”), from Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ (“side, flank, edge, shore”), derived from *sīdaz, probably from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“long, lasting”). The LGBTQ slang sense was coined by sex therapist and author Joe Kort in 2010 and popularized in 2013.
side.g: A bounding straight edge of a two-dimensional shape.

side.e: From Middle English side, syde, syd, from Old English sīd (“wide, broad, spacious, ample, extensive, vast, far-reaching”), from Proto-West Germanic *sīd, from Proto-Germanic *sīdaz (“drooping, hanging, low, excessive, extra”), from Proto-Indo-European *sēy- (“to send, throw, drop, sow, deposit”).
side.g: Wide; large; long, pendulous, hanging low, trailing; far-reaching.

sided.g: Having the specified type of side or sides or number of sides.

siding.g: A building material which covers and protects the sides of a house or other building.

siding.e: From side + -ing (“derivative noun, having the quality of”).
siding.g: A second, relatively short length of track just to the side of a railroad track, joined to the main track by switches at one or both ends, u

siege.e: From Middle English sege, from Old French sege, siege, seige (modern French siège), from Vulgar Latin *sēdicum, from Latin sēdicŭlum, sēdēcula (“small seat”), from Latin sēdēs (“seat”). The military sense of the term is derived from the notion of an army "sitting down" in front of its target.

sieve.e: From Middle English sive, syfe, from Old English sife, from Proto-West Germanic *sibi (“sieve”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyp-, *seyb- (“to pour, sieve, strain, run, drip”).
sieve.g: A device with a mesh, grate, or otherwise perforated bottom to separate, in a granular material, larger particles from smaller ones, or to s

sift.e: From Middle English syften, from Old English siftan, from Proto-West Germanic *siftijan.

sigh.e: From Middle English sighen (“to sigh”), back-formation from sighte, past tense form of siken, from Old English sīcan, from Proto-West Germanic *sīkan, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *seykʷ- (“to pour out”).
sigh.g: To inhale a larger quantity of air than usual, and immediately expel it; to make a deep single audible respiration, especially as the result

sigh.e: From Middle English sighe (“sigh”), from sighen (“to sigh”) (see ).
sigh.g: A deep, prolonged audible inhale and exhale of breath; as when fatigued, frustrated, grieved, or relieved; the act of sighing.

sighing.e: From Middle English sighynge. By surface analysis, sigh + -ing.
sighing.g: Accompanied by or uttered with a sigh.

sight.e: From Middle English sighte, from Old English sihþ (“something seen; vision”), from Proto-West Germanic *sihti (“seeing, sight”), equivalent to see + -t.
sight.g: The sense or faculty by which objects are perceived through the agency of light; the sense by which we see.

sign.e: From Middle English signe, sygne, syng, seine, sine, syne, from Old English seġn (“sign; mark; token”) and Old French signe, seing (“sign; mark; signature”); both from Latin signum (“a mark; sign; token”); root uncertain. Partially displaced native token.
sign.g: A visible fact that shows that something exists or may happen.

sign.e: From Middle English signen, seinen, seinien, partly from Old English seġnian (“to mark; sign”) and partly from Anglo-Norman seigner, seiner et al., Old French signer et al., and their source Latin signāre (“to mark, seal, indicate, signify”); all from Latin signum (“a mark, sign”); see Etymology 1, above.

signal.e: From Old French segnal, seignal or Medieval Latin signāle; noun use of the neuter of Late Latin signālis, from Latin signum; verb use from 1805, as a shortened from signalize (1650s).
signal.g: A sequence of states representing an encoded message in a communication channel.

signature.e: Borrowed from Middle French signature, or from Medieval Latin signātūra, future active periphrastic of verb signāre from signum (“sign”), + -tūra, feminine of -tūrus, future active periphrastic suffix.
signature.g: A person's name, written by that person, used as identification or to signify approval of accompanying material, such as a legal contract.

signet.e: From Old French signet (“small seal”), from Medieval Latin signētum, diminutive of Latin signum (“sign”).
signet.g: An object (especially a ring) formerly used to impress a picture into the sealing wax of a document as a proof of its origin.

significant.e: From Latin significans, present participle of significare, from signum (“sign”) + ficare (“do, make”), variant of facere.

signification.e: From Old French significacion, from Latin significātiō.
signification.g: The act of signifying, or something that is signified; significance.

signify.e: From Middle English signifien, from Old French signifier, from Latin significare.
signify.g: To create a sign out of something.

signpost.g: A post bearing a sign that gives information on directions.

silence.e: From Middle English silence, from Old French silence, from Latin silentium (“silence”), from silēns (“quiet, silent”, present participle of silēre) + -ium.

silent.e: From Latin silēns (“silent”), present participle of sileō (“be silent”), from Proto-Indo-European *seyl- (“still, windless, quiet, slow”).
silent.g: Free from sound or noise; absolutely still; perfectly quiet.

silk.e: From Middle English silk, sylk, selk, selc, from Old English sioloc, seoloc, seolc (“silk”). The immediate source is uncertain; it probably reached English via the Baltic trade routes (cognates in Old Norse silki (> Danish silke, Swedish silke (“silk”)), Russian шёлк (šolk), obsolete Lithuanian zilkai̇̃), all ultimately from Late Latin sēricus.
silk.g: A fine fiber excreted by the silkworm or other arthropod (such as a spider).

silly.e: From Middle English seely, sēlī, from Old English sǣliġ, ġesǣliġ (“lucky, fortunate”), from Proto-West Germanic *sālīg, from *sāli; equivalent to seel (“happiness, bliss”) + -y. The semantic evolution is “lucky” to “innocent” to “naive” to “foolish”.
silly.g: Laughable or amusing through foolishness or a foolish appearance.

silver.e: From Middle English silver, selver, sulver, from Old English seolfor, from Proto-West Germanic *silubr, from Proto-Germanic *silubrą (“silver”), of uncertain origin.
silver.g: A lustrous, white, metallic element, atomic number 47, atomic weight 107.87, symbol Ag.

silverling.g: Shekel or small silvern coin of little value.

silversmith.e: From Middle English silver smyth, from Old English seolforsmiþ (“silversmith”), from Proto-Germanic *silubrasmiþaz (“silversmith”), equivalent to silver + smith. Eclipsed non-native Middle English argentarie (“silversmith”) from Latin (faber) argentārius (“dealer in silver, silversmith”).
silversmith.g: A person who makes articles out of silver usually larger than jewellery.

similar.e: From French similaire, from Medieval Latin similaris, extended from Latin similis (“like”); akin to simul (“together”).
similar.g: Having traits or characteristics in common; alike, allied, comparable.

similitude.e: From Old French similitude, from Latin similitūdō. By surface analysis, similar + -itude.
similitude.g: Similarity or resemblance to something else.

simple.e: From Middle English symple, from Old French simple, from Latin simplex (“simple”, literally “onefold”) (as opposed to duplex (“double”, literally “twofold”)), from semel (“the same”) + plicō (“to fold”). Partially displaced native English onefold.
simple.g: Uncomplicated; lacking complexity; taken by itself, with nothing added.

simplicity.e: From Middle English simplicite, from Old French simplicite, from Latin simplicitās, from simplex (“simple”). By surface analysis, simple + -icity. Partially displaced native English onefoldness.
simplicity.g: The state or quality of being simple

simply.e: From Middle English symply, symplely; equivalent to simple + -ly, with *-lely simplified to -ly by haplology.
simply.g: In a simple way or state; considered in or by itself; without addition; alone.

sin.e: From Middle English synne, sinne, from Old English synn (“sin”), from Proto-West Germanic *sunnju, from Proto-Germanic *sunjō (“truth, excuse”) and *sundī, *sundijō (“sin”), from , from *h₁sónts ("being, true", implying a verdict of "truly guilty" against an accusation or charge), from *h₁es- (“to be”); compare Old English sōþ ("true"; see sooth).
sin.g: A violation of divine will or religious law.

sin.e: From Middle English synnen, modification of earlier syngen, from Old English syngian, from synniġ (“sinful”) + -ian.

since.e: From Middle English syns, synnes, contraction of earlier sithens, sithence, from sithen (“after, since”) ( + -s, adverbial genitive suffix), from Old English sīþþan, from the phrase sīþ þǣm (“after/since that (time)”), from sīþ (“since, after”) + þǣm dative singular of þæt.
since.g: From a specified time in the past.

sincere.e: From Middle French sincere, from Latin sincerus (“genuine”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together”) (whence English sam) + *ḱer- (“grow”) (whence Latin Ceres, the goddess of harvest, etymon of cereal). Not from sine (“without”) + cera (“wax”), which is a folk etymology; see Wikipedia page.
sincere.g: Genuine, honest, and free from pretense or deceit; heartfelt.

sincerely.e: From sincere + -ly, from Latin sincērus (“pure, clean, sound”).
sincerely.g: In a sincere or earnest manner; honestly.

sincerity.e: From Middle English sinceritie, from Old French sincerité and Medieval Latin sincēritās; both from Latin sincēritās, from sincērus + -tās. Equivalent to sincere + -ity.
sincerity.g: The quality or state of being sincere.

sinew.e: From Middle English synwe, synewe (“tendon; ligament or other connective tissue; muscle; nerve; leaf vein”), from Old English sinu (“tendon, sinew; nerve”), from Proto-West Germanic *sinu, from Proto-Germanic *sinwō, from Proto-Indo-European *snéh₁wr̥ (“sinew, tendon”), from *(s)neh₁- (“to twist (threads), spin, weave”).
sinew.g: A cord or tendon of the body.

sinful.e: From Middle English synful, senful, sunful, from Old English synful (“sinful, guilty, wicked, corrupt”), equivalent to sin + -ful.

sing.e: From Middle English syngen, from Old English singan (“to sing”), from Proto-West Germanic *singwan, from Proto-Germanic *singwaną (“to sing”), from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷʰ- (“to recite, sing”).
sing.g: To produce musical or harmonious sounds with one’s voice.

singe.e: From Middle English sengen, from Old English senġan, sænċġan (“to singe, burn slightly, scorch, afflict”), from Proto-West Germanic *sangijan (“to burn, torch”), from Proto-Indo-European *senk- (“to burn”).

singer.e: From Middle English syngere, syngere, singere, equivalent to sing + -er.
singer.g: A person who sings, often professionally.
A person who, or device which, singes.

singing.e: From Middle English syngyng; equivalent to sing + -ing.
singing.g: The act of using the voice to produce musical sounds; vocalizing.

single.e: From Middle English single, sengle, from Old French sengle, saingle, sangle, from Latin singulus, a diminutive derived from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“one”).
single.g: Not accompanied by anything else; one in number.

singular.e: From Middle English singuler, from Old French, from Latin singulāris (“alone of its kind”), from Latin singulus (“single”).
singular.g: Being only one of a larger population; single, individual.

sink.e: From Middle English synken, from Old English sincan, from Proto-West Germanic *sinkwan, from Proto-Germanic *sinkwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sengʷ- (“to fall, sink”). In the causative sense, it replaced Old English senċan (“make sink”) from Proto-Germanic *sankwijaną.
sink.g: To move or be moved into something.

sinner.e: From Middle English synnere, equivalent to sin + -er.
sinner.g: A person who sins or has sinned.

sir.e: From Middle English sir, unstressed form of sire, borrowed from Old French sire (“master, sir, lord”), from Latin senior (“older, elder”), from senex (“old”).
sir.g: A man of a higher rank or position.

sister.e: From Middle English suster, from Old English sweostor, from Proto-West Germanic *swester, from Proto-Germanic *swestēr, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr. In standard English, the form with i is due to contamination with Old Norse systir (“sister”). The plural sistren is from Middle English sistren, a variant plural of sister, suster (“sister”).
sister.g: A daughter of the same parents as another person; a female sibling.

sister-in-law.e: From Middle English suster-in-lawe; equivalent to sister + -in-law.
sister-in-law.g: A female relative of one's generation, separated by one degree of marriage:

sistrum.e: Borrowed from Latin sīstrum, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σεῖστρον (seîstron), from σείω (seíō, “shake”).
sistrum.g: An ancient Egyptian musical instrument, to be shaken, consisting of a metal frame holding percussive metal beads.

sit.e: From Middle English sitten, from Old English sittan, from Proto-West Germanic *sittjan, from Proto-Germanic *sitjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *sed- (“sit”).
sit.g: To be in a position in which the upper body is upright and supported by the buttocks.

site.e: From Middle English site, from Anglo-Norman site, from Latin situs (“position, place, site”), from sinere (“to put, lay, set down, usually let, suffer, permit”).
site.g: The place where anything is fixed; situation; local position

sith.e: From Middle English sith (“journey, movement, lifetime, period, occasion”), from Old English sīþ (“journey, movement, trip, point in time, occasion”), from Proto-West Germanic *sinþ, from Proto-Germanic *sinþaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sent- (“to go, head”).
Clipping of sithen; compare German seit (“since”).

sitting.e: From Middle English sittinge, sittynge, variant of sittinde, sittende, sittande, from Old English sittende (“sitting”), from Proto-Germanic *sitjandz (“sitting”), present participle of Proto-Germanic *sitjaną (“to sit”), equivalent to sit + -ing.

situate.e: Borrowed from Late Latin situātus, past participle of Medieval Latin situō (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”).
situate.g: To place on or into a physical location.

situation.e: From Middle English situacioun, situacion, from Middle French situation, from Medieval Latin situatio (“position, situation”), from situare (“to locate, place”), from Latin situs (“a site”). By surface analysis, situate + -ion.
situation.g: The combination of circumstances at a given moment; a state of affairs.

six.e: From Middle English six, from Old English six, from Proto-West Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs. Toilet sense predates military usage.
six.g: A numerical value equal to 6; the number following five and preceding seven. This number of dots: (••••••).

sixteen.e: From Middle English sextene, sixtene, from Old English sixtīene, from Proto-Germanic *sehstehun. Equivalent to six + -teen.
sixteen.g: The cardinal number occurring after fifteen and before seventeen, represented in Arabic numerals as 16 and in Roman numerals as XVI.

sixteenth.e: From Middle English sixtenthe, sixtethe, from Old English sixtēoþa, equivalent to sixteen + -th.
sixteenth.g: The ordinal form of the number sixteen.

sixth.e: From earlier sixt, from Middle English sixte, from Old English siexta, from Proto-Germanic *sehstô. By surface analysis, six + -th (ordinal suffix).
sixth.g: The ordinal form of the number six.

sixty.e: From Middle English sixty, sexty, Old English sixtiġ, from Proto-Germanic *sehs tigiwiz (“sixty”), equivalent to six + -ty.
sixty.g: The cardinal number occurring after fifty-nine and before sixty-one, represented in Roman numerals as LX and in Arabic numerals as 60.

sixtyfold.e: From Middle English sixtifold, sexti fold, from Old English sixtiġfeald (“sixtyfold”), equivalent to sixty + -fold.
sixtyfold.g: By a multiple of sixty; by sixty times as much or as many.

size.e: From Middle English syse, of unclear origin; related to Old Italian sisa (“a glue used by painters”), perhaps ultimately related to size / syse (“amount”), or perhaps shortened from assisa, from assiso (“to make to sit, to seat, to place”)
size.g: A thin, weak glue used as primer for paper or canvas intended to be painted upon.
